The frequency used for the measurements was 25.9 MHz, corresponding to a wavelength of 38 feet.
The transmitter was located 300 feet from the target, which was assumed to provide plane-wave illumination for targets up to 30 feet long.
The probe was typically located 20 to 60 feet from the target, and did not receive plane waves from the target.

The standing-wave method was adapted for use at high frequencies by using a probe with its own detector, voltage comparator, and telemeter to eliminate the need for a cable from the probe to the control room.
The relative amplitude of the backscattered field was measured at various ranges from the target, and a standard range-dependence curve was fitted to the data.
The known cross section of a half-wave dipole was used to calibrate the system.
The results for the aluminum dipoles, including the variation of cross section with target length and the resonant frequencies, were consistent with the predictions from microwave measurements.
The effective height of the trees could be deduced from the measurements, suggesting that the scattering from the trees was dominated by the main trunk and branches.

The agreement between the high-frequency results for conducting dipoles and the microwave measurements demonstrated the validity of extrapolating microwave data to the high-frequency part of the spectrum.
Field strength measurements along lines perpendicular to the transmitter-target line provided additional insights into the scattering behavior of the targets.
The standing-wave method was used to measure the cross sections of trees, street lights, and vehicles, in addition to aluminum dipoles.
The lack of a good image plane at high frequencies required the use of methods to handle the range dependence and non-uniform illumination of the targets.

The relative power gain of the transmitting antenna at different heights above the ground was measured to account for the variation in illumination of vertical targets.
